clue.text: Under one's thumb? But here's the twist

definitions.text: Under one's thumb? But here's the twist

parts.words: Under one's thumb? But here's the twist
parts.note: the digit sitting just past the thumb on the hand, and the one people proverbially twist others round

explanation.surface: Someone seems firmly controlled, but a plot twist is coming.
explanation.walkthrough: Look along the hand: the smallest digit lies beyond (under) the thumb, and to 'twist someone round your little finger' is to control them completely.
explanation.definitionFit: The smallest digit of the hand, famous from the idiom about twisting a person round it.

clue.text: Annual consumers cut loss as arranged

indicators.note: the letters are set out in a new arrangement

explanation.surface: Annual subscribers trim their losses by agreement.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Annual' suggests a yearly subscription; swarming insects arrive yearly and consume crops.
explanation.definitionFit: Swarms of grasshoppers come seasonally and devour crops, so they are yearly eaters.

clue.text: Inseparable companion for Herrick's Rose

parts.note: Robert Herrick's poem 'The Rose' notes that no rose grows without its sharp prickly partner

explanation.surface: A poet's sweetheart named Rose has a constant companion.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rose' looks like a woman's name, but Herrick wrote of the flower and the spike that always grows on its stem.
explanation.definitionFit: A prickle on the stem always accompanies the flower, as the proverb about no rose without one says.

clue.text: Final play that is sure to be tricky

definitions.text: Final play that is sure to be tricky

parts.words: Final play that is sure to be tricky
parts.note: in card games, the closing card of the winning suit is sure to take a trick; also the Judgment Day trumpet call

explanation.surface: A closing stage drama is bound to be difficult.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Play' suggests a drama and 'tricky' difficult, but at whist or bridge a trump takes a trick; the phrase also names the trumpet blast of Judgment Day.
explanation.definitionFit: The final card of the trumps suit wins its trick, and the trumpet sounding Judgment Day is the ultimate call.

clue.text: Fibre needed-state number

parts.note: Fla is the abbreviation for the US state of Florida
X is the Roman numeral ten

explanation.surface: A form asks for a dietary fibre requirement and a state ID number.
explanation.definitionFit: Flax yields the fibre spun into linen.

clue.text: Little one settling comfortably

explanation.surface: A small child snuggles down cosily.
explanation.definitionFit: A baby bird still in its nest is a little one; snuggling down cosily is settling comfortably.

clue.text: There's nothing in one of the sins of a diplomat

indicators.note: the round letter for nothing is placed inside the word for the sin

parts.note: envy is one of the seven deadly sins
O, the zero, stands for nothing

explanation.surface: A diplomat is free of every deadly sin.
explanation.definitionFit: An envoy is a diplomatic representative sent abroad.

clue.text: Go for a rise in downright overclaiming

indicators.note: the turned word is placed inside the word for downright

parts.note: arrant means downright, utter

indicators.note: in a down entry a rise means the word reads upward, so backwards

explanation.surface: Someone pushes for a pay rise with blatant exaggeration.
explanation.walkthrough: 'For a rise' turns GO upward into OG, and 'in' puts OG inside ARRANT.
explanation.definitionFit: Being haughty means claiming more importance than one has.

clue.text: Whence material for the building game

explanation.surface: Where do the supplies for a construction game come from?
explanation.definitionFit: Stone for building is dug from a pit, and hunted prey is game.

clue.text: Diana's ill-humour when booked?

parts.note: read as bad tempers (...), and as the place in the title of a Meredith novel about Diana

explanation.surface: A woman named Diana is grumpy whenever she has a reservation.
explanation.walkthrough: George Meredith's novel 'Diana of the Crossways' puts Diana in a book; 'cross ways' are bad-tempered moods.
explanation.definitionFit: Meredith's novel title pairs Diana with this place, and cross ways would be grumpy manners.

clue.text: Endless good quality fine art

indicators.note: the word for good quality loses its final letter, as if its tail end were cut off

parts.note: virtue is moral goodness, a good quality

explanation.surface: A dealer praises the excellence of some unending fine art.
explanation.definitionFit: Virtu is a taste for, or objects of, fine art and curios.

clue.text: Governors to satisfy fully about two points

indicators.note: the word for satisfy fully goes round the two compass points, wrapping them

parts.note: to sate is to satisfy completely
E and N, east and north, are two points of the compass

explanation.surface: Ruling officials seek to fully content people on a couple of issues.
explanation.definitionFit: A senate is a governing council, a body of governors.

clue.text: One helping to fill the house

definitions.text: One helping to fill the house

parts.words: One helping to fill the house
parts.note: a theatre audience is 'the house', so anyone buying a seat helps fill it

explanation.surface: Someone is helping populate a home.
explanation.walkthrough: 'House' suggests a home, but in a theatre it means the audience.
explanation.definitionFit: Theatre attenders make up the house, the audience in a playhouse.

clue.text: Without which salt is unseasonable

parts.note: recalls the Gospel line about salt that has lost its flavour being no use for seasoning

explanation.surface: Salt lacking something is out of season.
explanation.walkthrough: Matthew 5:13 asks what use salt is if it has lost its savour; 'unseasonable' here means unable to season food.
explanation.definitionFit: Savour is flavour or taste, the thing salt adds to food.

clue.text: Part of speech (an old man's confession) has too many words

parts.note: a verb is one of the parts of speech
an elderly person admitting 'I age'

explanation.surface: An elderly man's confession, part of a speech, rambles on.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is a predicate: the clue says that the word for wordiness 'has too many words'.
explanation.definitionFit: Verbiage is excessive wordiness, speech padded with needless words.

clue.text: Like the boys who ignored Garrick's warning?

definitions.text: Like the boys who ignored Garrick's warning?

parts.words: Like the boys who ignored Garrick's warning?
parts.note: Garrick's song 'Heart of Oak' tells the boys to be steady; ignoring that leaves them the opposite

explanation.surface: Some lads paid no heed to an actor's caution.
explanation.walkthrough: David Garrick wrote 'Heart of Oak', the Royal Navy march whose chorus runs 'Steady, boys, steady'.
explanation.definitionFit: Boys who disobeyed the call to stand firm would be wobbly, not firm.

clue.text: More subdued way of a conqueror

parts.note: tamer means more docile, more subdued
a lane is a narrow way or road

explanation.surface: A conqueror adopts a gentler manner.
explanation.definitionFit: Tamerlane, or Timur, was the 14th-century Central Asian conqueror.

clue.text: What to do with an egg? Beat it for a start!

definitions.text: What to do with an egg?

explanation.surface: Cooking advice: whisk the egg first.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Beat it' looks like a whisking instruction, but it means 'get away fast!'
explanation.definitionFit: Eggs may be mixed up in the pan when cooking; a hurried clamber or dash away is another sense.

clue.text: Tortoiseshell's dear in Italy, with deference to its finish

indicators.note: the second piece is added at the finish of the first, closing the word

parts.note: cara is Italian for dear
pace, from Latin, means with deference to someone's view

explanation.surface: A tortoiseshell cat is cherished in Italy and treated with respect to the end.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tortoiseshell' suggests a cat or a comb, but here it is the shell itself.
explanation.definitionFit: A carapace is the hard upper shell of a tortoise or turtle.

clue.text: Worsted in Bavaria

explanation.surface: Someone was defeated in southern Germany.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Worsted' looks like a verb meaning beaten, but it is the woollen fabric.
explanation.definitionFit: Coburg is a twilled worsted cloth, and a town in Bavaria.

clue.text: Workshop occupied by a striker

parts.note: a workplace held by someone who strikes, here a blacksmith hammering, not a worker on strike

explanation.surface: Industrial action: a protesting worker occupies a factory.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Striker' suggests a picket, but a blacksmith strikes iron with a hammer.
explanation.definitionFit: A blacksmith's forge is the workplace where metal is hammered.

clue.text: Agent has last two letters destroyed (from a Tibetan source)

indicators.note: the letters are broken up and reassembled in a new order

parts.note: Y and Z close the alphabet

explanation.surface: A spy's final two letters have been destroyed, the material traced to Tibet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Destroyed' mixes AGENT with YZ.
explanation.definitionFit: China's longest river rises in the Tibetan plateau.

clue.text: Clay pigeon's counterpart as flying missile ?

definitions.text: Clay pigeon's counterpart as flying missile

parts.words: Clay pigeon's counterpart as flying missile
parts.note: a clay pigeon is a flying target; its match is a thrown clay block, built of clay and a flier like a pigeon

explanation.surface: Something to throw that matches a shooting target.
explanation.walkthrough: Brick (fired clay) pairs with clay, and the bat (a flying creature) with the pigeon; together they name a thrown chunk of masonry.
explanation.definitionFit: A brickbat is a piece of brick hurled as a weapon, and figuratively a harsh criticism.

clue.text: Put in when the boat rocked gently?

definitions.text: Put in when the boat rocked gently?

indicators.note: the letters are set inside the run of two words

explanation.surface: Something is placed aboard as the boat sways softly.
explanation.walkthrough: A small anchor is put in the water, and the word is put in 'rocked gently'.
explanation.definitionFit: A kedge is a light anchor, dropped to steady or haul a boat.

clue.text: Barchester's dean locked his stable door in time

parts.words: locked his stable door in time
parts.note: unlike the proverb's owner who shuts the door after the horse has bolted, he locks up with his Arab horse still inside

explanation.surface: A cathedral dean had the foresight to secure his stable.
explanation.walkthrough: In Trollope's Barchester novels the dean is Dr Arabin; read his name as 'Arab in', the horse safely shut in before it could bolt.
explanation.definitionFit: Trollope made Francis Arabin dean of Barchester in 'Barchester Towers'.

clue.text: Instrument to outlaw John Anderson

parts.note: to ban is to outlaw
Burns's song 'John Anderson, my Jo' gives jo, Scots for sweetheart

explanation.surface: A tool used to outlaw a man named John Anderson.
explanation.walkthrough: Robert Burns's song opens 'John Anderson, my jo, John', jo meaning a beloved in Scots.
explanation.definitionFit: The banjo is a stringed musical instrument.

clue.text: With which one gets right on to the green

definitions.text: With which one gets right on to the green

parts.words: With which one gets right on to the green
parts.note: a golfer's approach shot onto the putting surface is played with this kind of club

explanation.surface: Someone finds the way straight onto the village green.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Green' suggests a village lawn, but it is golf's putting surface, reached with an approach club.
explanation.definitionFit: Golfers use the metal-headed club for approach shots to the putting surface.

clue.text: Swiss mountain many find unyielding?

parts.note: the Rigi is a mountain near Lucerne in Switzerland
D is the Roman numeral 500, a large number, so many

explanation.surface: Lots of climbers think a particular Alp is hard going.
explanation.definitionFit: Rigid means stiff and inflexible, refusing to bend.

clue.text: Rod's a local counter-attraction

parts.note: a pub (the local) has a bar counter that draws people in, and a magnetised rod attracts

explanation.surface: A man called Rod is the draw at the bar of the neighbourhood pub.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rod' looks like a drinker's name, and 'local' is the British word for a nearby pub; the counter there is a bar.
explanation.definitionFit: A straight magnetised rod, an attracting piece of metal, takes its name from being bar-shaped.

clue.text: Oh, free beer in distribution already indeed?

indicators.note: the letters of the phrase are dealt out afresh like beer being handed round

explanation.surface: Someone is surprised that free beer has already been handed out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In distribution' reads as one phrase, but 'in' belongs to the letters being rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: Legal documents use the word for 'earlier in this text', that is, mentioned already.
